content: Exercise training is frequently recommended for individuals diagnosed with fibromyalgia. This systematic review specifically investigated the effects of supervised group aquatic exercise programs, which are led by an instructor. Aquatic training was defined as physical exercise performed in a pool, with participants standing in water at waist, chest, or shoulder depth. This review is an update of the Exercise for treating fibromyalgia syndrome review, originally published in 2002 and updated in 2007. The primary objective of this review was to assess the benefits and potential harms of aquatic exercise training in adults with fibromyalgia. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, CINAHL, PEDro, and others, covering studies from their inception to October 2013. The search also included reference lists from key journals, identified articles, meta-analyses, and reviews of fibromyalgia treatments. Using Cochrane methods, citations, abstracts, and full-text articles were screened to identify relevant studies on aquatic exercise training. The inclusion criteria for this review required studies to be randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults diagnosed with fibromyalgia based on established criteria. The studies needed to provide between-group data comparing an aquatic intervention to a control or another intervention. Studies were excluded if less than 50% of the intervention involved exercise in water. Data collection and analysis involved independent assessment of the risk of bias and extraction of data for 24 outcomes, with seven designated as major outcomes: multidimensional function, self-reported physical function, pain, stiffness, muscle strength, submaximal cardiorespiratory function, withdrawal rates, and adverse effects. Discrepancies were resolved through discussion. Interventions were evaluated using mean differences (MD) or standardized mean differences (SMD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Meta-analyses were conducted when two or more studies provided data for a specific outcome. A 15% threshold was set to determine clinically relevant differences. The review included 16 studies involving 881 participants (866 women and 15 men). Nine studies compared aquatic exercise to a control group, five compared aquatic exercise to land-based exercise, and two compared different aquatic exercise programs. The risk of bias was rated as low for random sequence generation, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, blinding of outcome assessors, and other biases. However, the risk of bias for blinding of participants and personnel, as well as allocation concealment, was rated as low or unclear. Limitations in the evidence included imprecision, high statistical heterogeneity, and wide confidence intervals. Aquatic Exercise vs. Control: Statistically significant improvements were observed in all major outcomes for participants in aquatic exercise programs compared to control groups. On a 100-point scale: Multidimensional function improved by 6 units (MD -5.97, 95% CI -9.06 to -2.88; NNT 5, 95% CI 3 to 9). Self-reported physical function improved by 4 units (MD -4.35, 95% CI -7.77 to -0.94; NNT 6, 95% CI 3 to 22). Pain improved by 7 units (MD -6.59, 95% CI -10.71 to -2.48; NNT 5, 95% CI 3 to 8). Stiffness improved by 18 units (MD -18.34, 95% CI -35.75 to -0.93; NNT 3, 95% CI 2 to 24). Muscle strength, as measured by knee extension and hand grip, was 0.63 standard deviations higher in the aquatic group compared to the control group (SMD 0.63, 95% CI 0.20 to 1.05; NNT 4, 95% CI 3 to 12). Cardiovascular submaximal function improved by 37 meters on the six-minute walk test (95% CI 4.14 to 69.92). Among the major outcomes, only stiffness and muscle strength met the 15% threshold for clinical relevance, with improvements of 27% and 37%, respectively. Withdrawal rates were similar between the aquatic and control groups. Adverse effects were poorly reported, but no serious adverse effects were noted. Aquatic Exercise vs. Land-Based Exercise: No statistically significant differences were found between aquatic and land-based exercise for multidimensional function, self-reported physical function, pain, or stiffness. On a 100-point scale: Multidimensional function differed by 0.91 units (95% CI -4.01 to 5.83). Self-reported physical function differed by -5.85 units (95% CI -12.33 to 0.63). Pain differed by -0.75 units (95% CI -10.72 to 9.23). Stiffness differed by 2 units (95% CI -8.88 to 1.28). Submaximal cardiorespiratory function showed a difference of 3 seconds on a 100-meter walk test (95% CI -1.77 to 7.77). A statistically significant difference favoring land-based training was observed for muscle strength, with a 2.40 kilopascal increase in grip strength (95% CI 4.52 to 0.28). None of the outcomes in the aquatic vs. land-based comparison reached the 15% threshold for clinical relevance. Withdrawal rates were similar between the two groups, and adverse effects were poorly reported, with no serious adverse effects in either group. Aquatic Exercise vs. Aquatic Exercise (e.g., Ai Chi vs. Stretching, Pool Water vs. Sea Water): Among the major outcomes, the only statistically significant difference was for stiffness, which favored Ai Chi (1.00 on a 100-point scale, 95% CI 0.31 to 1.69). Conclusions: Lowto moderate-quality evidence suggests that aquatic exercise training is beneficial for improving overall wellness, symptoms, and physical fitness in adults with fibromyalgia when compared to no exercise. Very lowto low-quality evidence indicates that both aquatic and land-based exercise provide benefits, except for muscle strength, where very low-quality evidence favors land-based exercise. No serious adverse effects were reported in any of the included studies.
